standard.title: Post-War Australia — Development and International Relationships
standard.description: the significance of the Second World War to Australia's immediate post-war economic, political and social development, and Australia's international relationships in the 20th century
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied Australia's post-WWI international relationships and the significance of the war to Australian national identity, including the Anzac legend and Australia's role at the Paris Peace Conference.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate the significance of the Second World War to Australia's post-war development and international relationships, including the shift from Britain to the USA and deeper engagement with Asia.

nodes.label: Post-war reconstruction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe Australia's post-war reconstruction under Chifley and explain the key priorities of the post-war Labor government.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two priorities of post-war reconstruction under Chifley and explain the context that made reconstruction necessary.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the role of Prime Minister Ben Chifley in post-war reconstruction — the need to transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy, demobilisation, housing policy, the 'New Deal'-style approach to social infrastructure; explain the economic, political and social challenges of the immediate post-war period.
wider: Compare Chifley's reconstruction vision with that of the Curtin government's wartime planning, examining how wartime centralisation shaped post-war policy ambitions
Investigate the bank nationalisation controversy under Chifley as a case study in the limits of post-war Labor reform — examining how it contributed to Labor's defeat in 1949

response_modes.reason: Post-war reconstruction is often treated as background context. Give it substantive treatment — it explains why Australia was positioned to benefit from the long economic boom (K16) and why immigration was prioritised (K07).

success_criteria: Describe at least two priorities of post-war reconstruction under Chifley
Explain why post-war reconstruction was necessary and what challenges it needed to address
Identify at least one policy of the post-war Labor government and explain its purpose

nodes.label: Shifting alliances — Britain to the USA
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the significance of Australia's changing relationship with Britain and the USA after WWII, including the creation of the ANZUS alliance.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the shift in Australia's primary strategic relationship from Britain to the USA after WWII and describe the ANZUS alliance.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the significance of WWII to Australia's changing relationship with Britain and the USA — the fall of Singapore as the moment that demonstrated Britain could not defend Australia, Curtin's pivot to the USA, the post-war formalisation of the relationship through the ANZUS Treaty (1951); evaluate the long-term significance of this shift for Australian foreign and defence policy.
wider: Examine the negotiation of the ANZUS Treaty in depth — analysing what Australia gave and received, and how it was received differently by different political groups in Australia

Investigate how Australia's shift from Britain to the USA was reflected in popular culture, immigration policy, and trade patterns in the 1950s — examining how strategic realignment played out in everyday Australian life
nodes.hinge_reason: The strategic shift to the USA is foundational to understanding Australia's Cold War-era foreign policy, military commitments (Korea, Vietnam), and the ANZUS relationship that shapes K16 and K17. Students who see this as simply a wartime tactical shift rather than a fundamental realignment miss the logic of subsequent Australian foreign policy decisions.

response_modes.reason: The shift from Britain to the USA is often treated as inevitable; make the contingency explicit — what would Australia's strategic options have been if the USA had not entered the Pacific War? This counterfactual helps students understand the significance of the shift.

success_criteria: Explain why Australia's primary strategic relationship shifted from Britain to the USA after WWII
Describe the ANZUS alliance and explain its significance for Australian security
Evaluate the long-term importance of the Britain-to-USA shift for Australia's foreign policy

nodes.label: Engagement with Asia and the United Nations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate Australia's post-war engagement with Asia and its role in founding the United Nations.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two ways Australia deepened its engagement with Asia after WWII and explain Australia's role in the founding of the United Nations.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate Australia's deeper engagement with Asia — SEATO, the South Pacific Forum, APEC, the ASEAN Regional Forum, the Colombo Plan, various trade alliances; describe the involvement of Australia in founding the United Nations, including the roles of HV Evatt and Jessie Street in drafting the UN Charter; investigate the wave of post-war European and Asian migration, including the Colombo Plan, and the attitudes toward race that both drove and were challenged by this engagement.
wider: Investigate the Colombo Plan in depth — examining how Australia's engagement with Asian students and economies through the plan challenged and gradually shifted White Australia Policy attitudes

Examine Jessie Street's role in drafting the UN Charter alongside HV Evatt, analysing how her advocacy for women's rights was incorporated into the foundational UN documents — and how her contribution has been historically marginalised

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the strategic shift (Node 2) with Australia's broader multilateral engagements, completing the picture of post-war international repositioning. It also provides context for K07 (migration) and K08 (changing attitudes to migration).

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Jessie Street and the Colombo Plan both offer underexplored angles on the post-war international settlement that connect to gender history (K12) and the slow unravelling of the White Australia Policy (K07, K08).
success_criteria: Describe at least two ways Australia deepened its engagement with Asia after WWII
Explain Australia's role in founding the United Nations, naming at least one individual who contributed
Describe the post-war wave of migration and explain its connection to Australia's changing international relationships
